tldr: We propose WarpWeaver, a real-time planner that solves multi-robot coordination for differentially flat nonlinear systems by combining decentralized column generation with dispersive tree search. By negotiating rents on shared space, the robots reach near-globally optimal agreements in real time, even under asynchronous communication delays, as demonstrated in simulations and physical robot experiments.
hero_caption: Comparison between Iterated Best Response and the proposed method (Dispersive Tree Agreement). In (a), decentralized optimization falls into a local optimum, resulting in a total travel time of 17.5 s. In (b), our method negotiates space rents to reach a team-wide agreement, yielding mutually cooperative trajectories that achieve a near-globally optimal total time of 13.5 s.
overview:
Coordinating multiple nonlinear robots to avoid mutual collisions or maintain communication networks can be naturally formulated as a joint optimal control problem for the entire team. However, existing methods have been polarized into centralized offline planners that pursue joint optimality, and decentralized online planners that simplify dynamics and settle for local optima (safe navigation). No decentralized framework existed that could pursue joint optimality while coping with realistic communication delays and real-time deadlines.

To bridge this gap, the authors build on a single-robot dispersive tree search framework for differentially flat systems. They mathematically prove that inter-robot coupling can be absorbed by local corridor constraints, showing that locally grown dispersive trees inherently contain a near-optimal team-wide agreement. To efficiently discover this agreement, they decentralize column generation, a classical technique for large-scale integer programs. The resulting protocol, WarpWeaver, prices shared space using dual variables as rents and lets robots negotiate these rents to coordinate their motion.

In benchmarks on the Dynobench suite, WarpWeaver reduced total travel time by up to 22% compared to centralized offline planners, and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline (EGO-Swarm). Hardware experiments on six autonomous mobile robots computing onboard, as well as communication graph maintenance tasks, demonstrated its robustness: even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short, the resulting trajectories closely matched fully quiesced agreements.
contributions: Formulated differentially flat multi-robot coordination as dispersive tree search and theoretically proved that locally grown trees contain a near-optimal agreement for the entire team.
Constructed a decentralized column generation method where robots asynchronously negotiate rents on shared space via dual variables, with guaranteed near-optimality certified at quiescence.
Developed WarpWeaver, a receding-horizon protocol tolerant to communication delays that secures high-quality agreements under real-time deadlines.

Outperformed offline centralized and existing real-time planners in simulation travel time, and validated onboard real-time execution across six mobile robots running on Jetson Orin under tether constraints.

sections.heading: Moving beyond the dichotomy of offline centralized vs. local decentralized planners
sections.summary: This work aims to close the gap between centralized offline methods pursuing joint optimality and decentralized real-time methods focusing merely on safety. By extending single-robot dispersive tree search to multi-robot teams, the authors introduce WarpWeaver, a decentralized column generation protocol based on negotiating rents for shared space.
sections.details:
Coordinating a team of robots with nonlinear dynamics is naturally formulated as a Joint Optimal Control Problem (JOCP) over the combined joint state space. However, existing approaches suffer from a sharp dichotomy.

On one hand, centralized planners (such as multi-agent pathfinding or sampling-based algorithms) can guarantee asymptotic optimality under collision avoidance, but their high computational cost restricts them to offline use. On the other hand, decentralized planners (such as trajectory optimization or distributed MPC) treat other robots' predicted paths as dynamic obstacles in real time; however, they often rely on simplified dynamics and get trapped in local optima without pursuing joint optimality for the whole team.

This paper extends dispersive forward tree (DFT) search—which generates near-optimal inputs for differentially flat systems in polynomial time—to the multi-robot domain. The authors first show that by replacing complex inter-robot interactions with local corridor constraints, the Cartesian product of independently grown dispersive trees is guaranteed to contain a near-optimal agreement for the entire team.

To find this agreement efficiently, they decentralize column generation from mathematical programming. Dual variables on shared space occupancy define "rents," guiding each robot to generate and propose trajectory candidates (columns) from its own tree that offer the greatest improvement. WarpWeaver implements this negotiation over an asynchronous, receding-horizon framework.

captions.F1: Two robots crossing paths around an obstacle. In (a) Iterated Best Response, each robot takes the other's trajectory as fixed, resulting in a total time of 17.5 s for blue and red. In (b) our method, robots negotiate space rents to achieve joint optimality, passing each other in a total of 13.5 s.

sections.heading: From multi-agent path finding to distributed optimization and column generation
sections.summary: Existing multi-robot planning methods fall into sampling/search-based, trajectory optimization, or consensus-based approaches. This paper takes a distinct angle by decentralizing integer programming column generation and coupling it with tree search over differentially flat dynamics.
sections.details:
### II-A Sampling and Search-Based Multi-Robot Planning
Sampling-based approaches in the composite state space (such as composite PRMs) and multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) extended to continuous dynamics (e.g., db-CBS) guarantee completeness or optimality. However, most remain centralized and offline, limiting their applicability to dynamic environments in real time.

### II-B Trajectory Optimization and Distributed MPC
In decentralized trajectory optimization, each robot locally optimizes its trajectory around candidate paths received from others. Distributed Model Predictive Control (DMPC) and ADMM-based consensus methods are widely studied, but they rely on mismatch penalties or simplified models, often missing superior joint solutions for the entire team.

### II-C Coordination Beyond Collision Avoidance
Beyond simple mutual separation, tasks may involve team-wide constraints such as maintaining communication network connectivity (algebraic connectivity of graphs) or physical cable linkages (tether constraints). While prior works relied on specialized potential fields or heuristics, the proposed method handles arbitrary hard coupling constraints in a unified manner.

### II-D Column Generation and Distributed Pricing
Column generation is an optimization technique for solving massive linear programs by generating only the necessary variables (columns) on the fly. It searches for improving columns using dual variables (shadow prices) of the constraints as prices. The novelty of this work lies in distributing column generation across a multi-robot team and tying it directly to onboard dispersive tree search on each robot.

sections.heading: Joint optimal control and its reformulation via differential flatness
sections.summary: Multi-robot coordination is formulated as a Joint Optimal Control Problem (JOCP) minimizing a sum or maximum of individual costs. By leveraging the differential flatness of each robot's dynamics, state-input search is mapped into curve search over the flat output jet space.
sections.details:
### Problem Setup
Consider a team of $N$ robots. The nonlinear dynamics of each robot $i$ are given by $\dot{x}^i = f^i(x^i, u^i)$. Over a horizon $T$, the team solves for trajectories minimizing a joint cost $\Phi$, which is a convex piecewise-linear aggregation (such as a weighted sum or maximum) of individual costs $J_i$. The solution must satisfy individual constraints $\mathcal{G}_i$ (obstacle avoidance, terminal rest, etc.) and group coupling constraints $\mathcal{G}_e$ (inter-robot collision avoidance, communication connectivity, etc.).

### III-A Motivating Examples
The paper highlights two representative scenarios:
- Example 1 (Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance): Robots navigate toward goal regions while maintaining a pairwise distance of at least $R_i + R_j$.
- Example 2 (Network Connectivity): Robots and a base station must preserve communication ranges and line-of-sight conditions such that a spanning tree over the team is maintained at all times.

### III-B Flat Reformulation
Each robot is assumed to be differentially flat. Differential flatness implies that states and inputs can be expressed algebraically in terms of flat outputs and their time derivatives (the jet). This eliminates the need to explicitly integrate differential equations, transforming the search into finding curves directly in the output jet space.

sections.heading: Solving single-robot control near-optimally in polynomial time with dispersive trees
sections.summary: We review Dispersive Forward Trees (DFTs) for single-robot optimal control from prior work. Pruning the flat output space across a grid prevents exponential growth while generating trajectories with theoretical near-optimality guarantees in polynomial time.
sections.details:
To solve single-robot flat optimal control problems, the framework employs Dispersive Forward Trees (DFTs) from prior work (Deshpande et al., 2024).

Forward propagation of command sequences from an admissible control set $\mathcal{A}$ causes the tree to grow exponentially as $O(|\mathcal{A}|^T)$ with horizon $T$. DFT circumvents this by defining spatiotemporal cells with a pruning radius $s$. When multiple trajectory nodes fall into the same cell, only the node with the lowest accumulated cost is retained, and the others are pruned (de-duplication).

This pruning bounds the computational complexity to a polynomial order in horizon $T$: $O(|\mathcal{A}| T^{d+1} (M/s)^{|R|})$. Crucially, if the dispersion of the input set $\delta_{\mathcal{A}}$ and the pruning radius $s$ are sufficiently small, the suboptimality gap relative to the true optimum is bounded by at most $L_J \rho$, where $\rho$ is proportional to the discretization resolution (Theorem 1).

sections.heading: Decentralized column generation and real-time agreement via space rent negotiation
sections.summary: We show that locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement, formulated as an integer linear program and solved via decentralized column generation. Robots negotiate dual variable rents for shared space, reaching agreements asynchronously over a receding horizon with WarpWeaver.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B Existence of Near-Optimal Agreements
As a theoretical foundation, the authors prove that by establishing a corridor constraint of radius $\rho$ around each robot, coupling constraints can be decoupled into local constraints. Consequently, the Cartesian product of local dispersive trees $\prod_i \mathcal{T}_i$ is guaranteed to contain an agreement whose cost is within $L_\Phi \rho$ of the true team optimum (Proposition 1).

### V-C Discretization to an Integer Linear Program (ILP)
By discretizing space into cells of diameter $S$ and time with step $h$, the agreement problem is formulated as an Integer Linear Program (ILP) using "occupancy rows" that prohibit simultaneous cell occupancy violating coupling constraints.

### V-D Decentralized Column Generation
Enumerating all candidate trajectories (columns) beforehand is intractable. Instead, column generation is applied. Solving the linear relaxation over the current column pool (restricted master problem: $\mathrm{LP}(Q)$) yields dual variables ($\mathrm{DP}(Q)$), from which the rent $\mu_{i,\kappa,m}$ for occupying a spatiotemporal cell is derived.
Each robot $i$ solves a local pricing problem using onboard DFT search, minimizing its cost augmented by these rents. Robots naturally generate candidate trajectories avoiding high-rent conflict regions and add them to the pool. When no robot can find an improving column, the system reaches quiescence, certifying the near-optimality of the agreement (Theorem 2).

### V-E WarpWeaver Protocol and Real-Time Implementation
To run this negotiation in practice under communication delays $\delta_{\mathrm{comm}}$, the WarpWeaver protocol (Algorithm 1) is introduced. Robots run column generation loops asynchronously onboard and broadcast newly found columns. At the real-time deadline (commit time $t_n$), the best mutually acknowledged agreement is committed. Even if cut short before quiescence, WarpWeaver consistently yields exceptionally high-quality agreements.

sections.heading: Simulation benchmarks: Outperforming offline centralized and decentralized baselines
sections.summary: Evaluated on Dynobench benchmarks, 10-drone swarm flights, and communication connectivity tasks, WarpWeaver cut total travel time by up to 22% versus centralized offline planners and up to 37% versus real-time decentralized EGO-Swarm, with negligible loss from real-time deadline truncation.
sections.details:
### VI-A Multi-Robot Kinodynamic Motion Planning
WarpWeaver was evaluated on unicycle and 3D double integrator models from the Dynobench suite against state-of-the-art centralized offline planners (db-CBS, db-ECBS, db-PIBT, db-LaCAM). WarpWeaver succeeded in all trials, achieved the shortest total travel time in 10 out of 11 benchmarks, and reduced travel time by a median of 8% and up to 22% compared to the best baseline.

In an EGO-Swarm forest benchmark with 10 quadrotors (including high-fidelity X500 models), EGO-Swarm succeeded in only 12 of 15 runs, whereas WarpWeaver achieved a 100% collision-free success rate and reduced total travel time by 31% to 37%. In scaled emulation tests (10 to 50 robots), WarpWeaver achieved 17% to 35% shorter travel times than db-LaCAM given a 300 s offline budget.

### VI-B Communication Network Connectivity Maintenance
In a collaborative mapping task with four robots using LiDAR under communication constraints, WarpWeaver was compared against Realm, a domain-specific planner. WarpWeaver completed all 15 tasks (Realm completed 8 and failed entirely in forests), reducing arrival times by up to 59%. Behaviors such as early-arriving robots backtracking to serve as relays emerged naturally without hand-crafted rules.

### VI-C Impact of Real-Time Truncation
Comparing a deliberate mode (negotiating until complete quiescence) with real-time deadline truncation showed that deadline cuts caused travel time degradation of only 0.3% to 1.2% (and just a few percent in 50-robot instances). This confirms that truncating negotiation yields practically near-optimal trajectories.

sections.heading: Real-robot experiments: Onboard real-time coordination across six mobile robots
sections.summary: WarpWeaver was deployed fully onboard six mobile robots equipped with Jetson Orin computers over Wi-Fi. It succeeded collision-free across obstacle position swaps, doorway bottlenecks, and pairwise virtual tethering tasks.
sections.details:
To evaluate real-world feasibility, hardware experiments were conducted using six small mobile robots (two JR and four RR units). Each robot ran Algorithm 1 fully decentralized on an onboard Jetson Orin, exchanging messages via ROS 2 over Wi-Fi (one-way latency median 13 ms, 99th percentile 106 ms).

Three scenarios were evaluated over three consecutive trials each:
- Swap around four pillar obstacles.
- Tethered Swap, where two robot pairs had to maintain a distance under 2.4 m and line of sight.
- Doorway Swap, where two groups of three robots traversed an opposing 1.6 m narrow doorway.

All trials achieved goal arrival with zero collisions among robots or obstacles. In the tethered scenario, the maximum separation was 2.37 m, strictly honoring the 2.4 m limit. Tracking errors against planned trajectories remained low, averaging 0.03 m to 0.07 m. Across 312 planning commit cycles, robots agreed on the identical solution in 311 instances (the single mismatch occurred during a post-battery swap restart), verifying robustness against real-world packet jitter and delays.

(a) Position swap around four pillars, (b) swap under pairwise tether constraints (dashed lines), and (c) mutually cooperative crossing through a narrow doorway.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: Combining dispersive tree search with decentralized column generation achieves both real-time tractability and joint near-optimality in multi-robot coordination. Addressing tightly coupled tasks such as rigid formations remains a subject for future work.
sections.details:
This paper introduced WarpWeaver, a real-time protocol formulating differentially flat multi-robot coordination via decentralized column generation and dispersive tree search. The method provides theoretical near-optimality guarantees at quiescence while consistently delivering high-quality agreements under real-time truncation, as validated in simulations and physical experiments.

A limitation is that computational tractability relies on the tightness of the integer linear relaxation. In tasks with rigid equality constraints, such as maintaining rigid formations, the combinatorial space of admissible joint agreements shrinks drastically, weakening the LP relaxation. Future extensions may integrate derivative-based local geometric optimization into the dispersive tree search to better handle such tightly coupled constraints.

takeaways: Dispersive Forward Trees (DFTs) generate near-optimal trajectory candidates for differentially flat nonlinear dynamics in polynomial time.
Column generation for large integer programs can be naturally decentralized across robots by interpreting constraint dual variables as space rents.
Asynchronous negotiation maintains consensus despite communication delays, yielding trajectory quality under real-time deadlines that is nearly indistinguishable from full quiescence.
limitations: Tight geometric constraints that severely restrict relative robot motion, such as rigid formation maintenance, weaken the linear relaxation and degrade search efficiency.
The approach assumes differentially flat robot dynamics and cannot be directly applied to non-flat systems.
In extremely large teams or environments, the growing number of columns in the shared pool may increase the linear programming solve time, straining onboard computational limits.
